pages.title: Al-Andalus, Spain under Islamic Rule
pages.content:
Muslims ruled a large part of the Iberian Peninsula, present-day Spain and Portugal, from 711 to 1492. The lands under Muslim rule were known as Al-Andalus. Although their lands slowly got smaller after the 11th century, Muslims lived there for 781 years until only the Kingdom of Granada was left. In particular, during the first three centuries, they established the most advanced and brilliant civilization that the West had ever seen. Above all, they created numerous invaluable works in art, architecture, medicine, literature, and philosophy.

The region includes famous historic cities like Granada, Seville, and Córdoba. Today, it is known as Andalusia and is one of Spain’s 17 autonomous regions.

pages.title: The Muslim Conquest of Spain
pages.content: The history of Muslim Spain began in the early 8th century in the western Mediterranean, where Europe and Africa are very close. The Muslim conquerors came from Syria, Arabia, and Egypt. They were determined soldiers who were motivated by a strong belief. In 711, Tariq ibn Ziyad, the Berber (a people who live in North Africa) governor, started the conquest of the Iberian Peninsula with an army. The army was made up mostly of Berbers. (The Iberian Peninsula today includes Spain and Portugal.) In 711, Tariq ibn Ziyad captured Toledo, the capital city of the Visigoths. One year later, in 712, Musa ibn Nusayr joined him. Musa was the Umayyad governor of Ifriqiya. Ifriqiya is an area that is now Tunisia, eastern Algeria, and western Libya. Together, the two commanders moved very fast with their armies. They conquered most of Spain and Portugal in just three years. At that time, the Visigothic Kingdom in Spain faced many problems due to internal struggles for the throne, social unrest, and laws that forced Jews to become Christians. During the Muslim conquest, many people who were unhappy with Visigothic rule, especially the Jews, voluntarily opened their city gates to the Muslims. At that time, villagers were living a very hard life. Most people saw the Muslims as saviors and cooperated with them. Historians say that Spain had serious internal weaknesses. Because of these problems, Muslims conquered the country very easily.

pages.title: A Cultural Golden Age
pages.content:
When the famous traveler Ibn Jubayr was born in Valencia in 1145, Muslim Spain was enjoying a cultural golden age. This lively era produced brilliant thinkers like the philosopher and scientist Ibn Rushd, the physician Ibn Tufayl, and the Sufi writer Ibn al-Arabi. In the 10th century, Granada was far more prosperous than most cities in the east. During the same period, Seville had 500 bathhouses and 1,000 mosques. Córdoba had a population of 300,000 to 500,000 and was the biggest city in Western Europe. This high level of development deeply impressed the Christians in the Middle Ages, who lived a much simpler life. Islamic Spain clearly stood out because of its advanced culture, while the rest of Western Europe was in a dark and poor period. Al-Andalus developed a unique culture because it mixed European, Asian, and African traditions. This combination gave the region a strong identity, so it was quite different from the rest of the Islamic world. Actually, the influence of eight centuries of Islamic rule in the region continued even after Christians took it back.

In this region, not only did different cultures meet, but two different social and economic systems also came together. The first, the Islamic community, was urban. They did business through a large trade network that connected to the Mediterranean and areas beyond, and they used a money economy. The second group, the Christians, was a rural society and lived mainly in the countryside. Also, with this conquest, the Mediterranean Sea, called the ‘Roman Lake’, turned from a closed sea into a global trade route which was linked to the Indian Ocean.

pages.title: The Umayyad State in Al-Andalus
pages.content: The conquest of Al-Andalus marks the final stage of the early Islamic conquests. By 710, Muslims had conquered almost all of North Africa, except for a few cities and fortresses. Therefore, it was natural that their next move was towards the Iberian Peninsula. In 750, the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads. However, the Umayyad dynasty started a new era in Al-Andalus in 756. They ruled the region for 275 years until their reign ended in 1031. During this time, the Umayyad throne of Al-Andalus changed hands 19 times. From the first emir, Abd al-Rahman I (756–788), to Abd al-Rahman III (912–961), rulers worked hard to keep the peace and build a culture where different ethnic groups could live together. The population of Islamic Spain was highly diverse. It consisted of Arabs, Berbers, and new converts to Islam. In fact, these new converts quickly became more numerous than the Arab Muslims. The local Spanish people also formed a large part of society, and they came from a mix of Roman and Visigoth ancestors. Additionally, Slavs, Christians, and Jews lived together in the same region.

pages.title: Abd al-Rahman III and the Golden Age
pages.content:
The reign of Abd al-Rahman III was the golden age of Al-Andalus. He rebuilt the power of the state at home and in the eyes of the Christian kingdoms. He launched more attacks on Christian lands in 951. After these attacks, the northern Christian states had to make peace with Abd al-Rahman III and pay a tax every year. In this period, the Abbasid caliphs lost their political and religious power. Therefore, Abd al-Rahman III claimed the title of caliph in 929 to lead the Islamic world. Around that time, in 909, the Shi’i Fatimids also announced their own caliphate in North Africa.

To compete with the Fatimids and the Byzantines in world trade, Abd al-Rahman III made his own gold coins. Even major powers like Constantinople, the Kingdom of Germany, and the Kingdom of France formed diplomatic ties with Abd al-Rahman and sent ambassadors to his court.

He supported the middle class and boosted trade and industry. He wanted to bring different ethnic groups together and reduce the power of the old Arab upper class, whose arrogant attitude was ruining the country’s peace. Abd al-Rahman III used foreign fighters in his army and gave important positions in the government to Christian slaves and Berbers instead of Arabs. By doing this, he successfully reduced the power of the traditional Arab nobles. Meanwhile, the native Spanish people, who were tired of Arab nobility rather than Islamic rule, grew stronger. For example, in the mid-10th century, a Jewish doctor named Hasday ibn Shaprut served in the caliph’s court. Through this policy, Abd al-Rahman III united all ethnic groups into a single, true nation: the Andalusians. After the Umayyad dynasty fell, the region split into small states during the Era of the Small Sultanates (1031–1090). Al-Andalus lost its political unity as almost every city declared independence, which led to different groups taking control of various areas.

pages.title: The Small Sultanates and the Reconquista
pages.content: Before 1031, the Muslims of Al-Andalus were united under a single state. However, after this date, the new local rulers cared mostly about defending their own borders. To survive, they even started asking the Christian kingdoms in the north for military help. For example, the rulers of Toledo made an alliance with the Kingdom of Castile to get an advantage over their rivals. This situation caused the Muslims to lose their power in the region step by step. On the other hand, it gave the Christian kingdoms a great chance to start the ‘Reconquista’, which means taking Al-Andalus back from the Muslims. Soon, King Ferdinand I of Castile brought these sultanates under his control. The capture of Toledo in 1085 was a major defeat for Muslims in Al-Andalus and a huge victory for Christians. At the time, Muslim rulers were fighting each other and did not see the Christian threat. Losing this important city finally made them realize the real danger of the Reconquista. By the mid-11th century, the Reconquista took on the nature of a crusade. In this situation, the Muslim states in Spain continued to survive with military support from North African Berber dynasties against the Christian kingdoms. Christian kingdoms took advantage of the weak situation in Al-Andalus. By 1236, they captured Córdoba. During this chaos, the Sultanate of Granada (1231–1492) was founded in the southeast.

pages.title: The Fall of Granada
pages.content:
In 1248, a Christian king captured Seville. After this date, there were still many Muslims living in the Christian kingdoms. They formed completely different communities, and many were hard-working peasants in the country districts.

In 1469, a major turning point happened in Spanish history. With the marriage of the Catholic Monarchs, the kingdoms of Aragon and Castile were united under a single royal house. This unification helped Christianity spread much faster across the region. Finally, in 1492, the last Muslim kingdom fell, and Islamic rule in the area ended.

pages.title: The Inquisition and Forced Conversion
pages.content:
After 1492, life changed completely for Muslims in Spain. They were forced to choose between becoming Christian or leaving the country. Many people were sent into exile, and Christian families settled in their houses. The Muslims who stayed behind had to live in separate, isolated neighborhoods outside the cities. The pressure was so strong that it was almost impossible to stay without accepting the Christian faith.

After 1499, the Spanish government started a strict policy to create one religion and one identity for the whole country. At first, they tried to persuade Muslims to convert to Christianity, and this method had some success. However, church leaders soon became impatient because they thought the process was too slow. As a result, they established the Inquisition in Granada in 1499 and began changing local mosques into churches.

To speed up the Christianization of the country, the government made a series of strict laws to completely eliminate Islamic culture. First, they closed all the butcher shops that sold halal meat. Soon after, speaking Arabic, using Arabic names, and owning Arabic books became illegal. The government also banned circumcision and traditional Islamic clothes. Finally, they ordered that all children under the age of six must be sent to monasteries to be raised as Christians. They made sure that all babies were born under the care of Christian midwives and were properly baptized right away. (Baptism: a Christian religious ceremony that marks a person’s entry into the faith.) Parents were also forced to choose only traditional Christian names for their children. On top of that, couples had to learn the Catholic faith from religious leaders before they could get married.

One major everyday habit that separated Muslims from Christian communities was using public baths. Because of this, orders were given to destroy them. Officials demanded that all public and private baths be destroyed, and anyone who disobeyed faced heavy fines or prison.

pages.title: Ottoman Aid and the Final Exile
pages.content:
The conquest of Constantinople in 1453 brought great joy to the Sultanate of Granada. For this last Islamic state in Al-Andalus, it meant the rise of a new, powerful Muslim force that could help them against Christian kingdoms.

In 1487, the ruler sent a messenger to the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid II to ask for help against Christian kingdoms, which were capturing their cities one by one. However, Bayezid II could not send help. He was too busy with his brother Cem and with the Mamluks. Instead, he wrote letters to the Pope and King Ferdinand II to ask them not to oppress the Muslims, but these efforts had no effect.

In 1502, ten years after the fall of Granada, the Muslims who stayed in the city sent another messenger to Bayezid II. The messenger explained their situation. He talked about the religious persecution and helplessness of the Muslims in Andalusia. In response, Bayezid II sent a fleet to the Mediterranean under the famous commander Kemal Reis. Kemal Reis attacked the Spanish coast and rescued a group of Muslims.

In 1525 and 1526, similar actions were taken against Muslims in other provinces. After 1526, everyone who lived in Spanish regions like Granada, Castile, Valencia, Aragon, and Catalonia was officially considered Christian. From that moment on, there were officially no Muslims left in Spain.

Between 1609 and 1614, Spain forced almost all Muslims to leave the country. The Ottoman Sultan, Ahmed I, could not help because he was already busy fighting wars against Austria and Iran. On top of that, his navy was not strong enough. However, he did not give up. He sent officials to Morocco, England, France, and Venice to ask for help for the Muslims of Al-Andalus. Thanks to his efforts, many Andalusians managed to escape and find a safe new home in North Africa and Istanbul.

pages.title: Society and Convivencia
pages.content:
In the Middle Ages, people did not have our modern idea of nations. Instead, society was divided by religion, so Al-Andalus had two main groups: Muslims and non-Muslims. The Muslim group included Arabs, Berbers, and new Muslims. These new Muslims were native Iberian people who converted to Islam after the conquest. The non-Muslim groups in the region were Christians and Jews.

According to historians, at the start of the 9th century, about half a million Arabs and Berbers lived in Al-Andalus. From the mid-9th century, most Muslims in Al-Andalus were local people who had converted to Islam, rather than Arab or Berber immigrants.

Under the agreements in the conquered areas, Christians were allowed to keep their religion, places of worship, and traditions. Their lives and property were also safe. In return, they paid a tax called the jizya (cizye), and those who owned land paid a land tax too.

Over time, the Christian people in Spain started to live like Muslims. They used Arabic for speaking and writing, and they adopted Muslim clothes, food, and daily habits. Because of this, people called them “Arabized.” They held important positions in the government and the military, and they had a big role in daily life and culture. They spoke both Arabic and Latin, and they also understood Islamic culture well. For this reason, they became a bridge that helped share ideas between Al-Andalus, Christian Spain, and the rest of Europe.

By the end of the Visigothic period, Jews had lost all their religious rights and became enslaved. With the Islamic conquest, they were able to live as a religious community and win back the right to practice their religion freely.

When discussing the history of Al-Andalus, the term Convivencia is essential. This Spanish word means “coexistence” or “living together.” It describes how Muslims, Christians, and Jews interacted politically, socially, and economically between 711 and 1492. Historians say the Islamic culture of Al-Andalus was confident and open enough to include non-Islamic elements. Indeed, in the 10th century, Córdoba was Europe’s biggest and most international city. Its population was between 300,000 and 500,000 and included Muslims, Christians, and Jews.

In Al-Andalus, people from any social background could hold almost any high position. The only exception was the position of head of state, which was only for the royal family.

Al-Andalus became the richest and most crowded place in Europe under Abd al-Rahman III. The capital, Córdoba, amazed the world with its Great Mosque, baths, and busy markets. The German poetess Hrotsvitha called it “the ornament of the world.”

pages.title: Economic Life
pages.content:
Cities like Seville, Toledo, Zaragoza, Granada, and Valencia also reached the same level of growth. When times were peaceful, the government’s income grew steadily. This wealth came from steady progress in farming, trade, and factories. In addition, people made great improvements in irrigation systems for crops. Muslims also brought new crops to Spain. They grew rice, sugarcane, apricots, oranges, pomegranates, and cotton there.

The production of wool, cotton, and silk textiles was very successful. In fact, historians said there were 13,000 textile makers in Córdoba alone. Coastal cities exported products like cotton, olives, olive oil, saffron, figs, and sugar to North Africa, the Byzantine Empire, and Egypt. From these places, traders moved the goods to other Asian countries.

Islamic rule in Al-Andalus ended completely in 1492. However, Muslims continued to have an important role in the economic life of Christian Spain for some time.

pages.title: Science, Culture, and the West
pages.content:
After the Islamic conquest, six million local people in Spain spoke Vulgar Latin, which was an early form of the language that later created Spanish, Portuguese, and Catalan. A small group of Arabs and Berbers spoke their own languages. Over time, however, more people started speaking Arabic because new immigrants moved from the East and married local women. New Muslims spoke both Arabic and their old local language, which they used together every day. Arabic was the official language and schools taught in it. Therefore, it became the common spoken and written language for all.

Europe rediscovered the works of Aristotle, Plato, Hippocrates, Galen, Ptolemy, and Euclid thanks to Arabic translations and commentaries written by Muslim scholars and philosophers. These texts were brought back to Muslim Spain and served as a source of inspiration for Europe’s Renaissance. Knowledge flowed in one direction: from the libraries of Cairo and Baghdad to Muslim Spain, and from there to the rest of Europe. Many Christian scholars traveled south to Muslim Spain in pursuit of knowledge.

Muslims in Al-Andalus used the knowledge of classical-period scholars in physiology and anatomy, and they even corrected some of their mistakes. They also improved practical medicine and wrote important books about surgical instruments and how to use them. In addition, they developed techniques to get essences from plants. They made contributions to pharmacology and opened pharmacies. Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, an expert in medicine and chemistry, wrote a thirty-volume medical encyclopedia called al-Tasrif. There were many hospitals in Al-Andalus. It is known that during the Caliphate period, there were about fifty hospitals of different sizes in Córdoba alone.

While Al-Andalus was building a bright and advanced civilization, Western Europe was going through a dark time. Europe did not know much about the progress which was made by Muslims. In the 11th century, the Crusades started in the East and Al-Andalus. This gave Christians a chance to see Islamic civilization up close. To learn more about it, they started translating Arabic books into their own languages. European scholars translated many Arabic books on science and philosophy into Latin. Sicily and Spain were the main places for this work. Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators worked together in special schools to translate books about math, medicine, astronomy, and philosophy.

Al-Andalus had a big impact on European architecture. Muslims built underground canals. This system helped reduce water loss. From the 12th century, Spanish and Portuguese kings copied the palaces of Córdoba. These buildings are very important for world art. They are rare today, but they show the finest Islamic style in Europe.

pages.title: Architecture and the Legacy of Al-Andalus
pages.content:
Here are a few examples:

The Great Mosque of Córdoba has a long and interesting history. In the past, it was a huge mosque, and it was the third-largest mosque in the Islamic world. Today, the building is a Christian church, and people call it the Córdoba Cathedral.

Madinat al-Zahra Palace was built by Caliph Abd al-Rahman III. Workers used 4,300 columns for the building. Most columns came from cities in Al-Andalus. About one-fourth of them came from places like Carthage, Tunis, Constantinople, and Frankish lands.

The Alhambra Palace in Granada is a very important building for Andalusian architecture and Islamic art. People call it “al-hamra” because this word means “red.” The palace has this name because the clay in its walls is reddish. Its history as a military fort started in the 9th century. However, the famous courtyards with pools, decorated halls, and royal palaces were built in the 13th and 14th centuries.

The Alcazar of Seville is a famous royal palace located in the center of Seville. Its name comes from the Arabic word al-qasr, which means “the palace.” The building is still a wonderful example of traditional craftsmanship today.

The following key facts show how special Andalusian civilization was for its time.

Caliph Al-Hakam II loved learning so much that he built a large library with over 400,000 books during his rule from 961 to 976.

Before the rise of Islamic medicine, European medical practices were very primitive. Even in the 1200s, hospitals in Europe could not match the high standards of Muslim medical centers.

A major turning point came when Ibn Sînâ’s masterwork, al-Qanun fi’t-Tibb, was translated into Latin in Toledo, Spain, during the 12th century.

Ibn Hazm (994–1064) was a very important scholar of Al-Andalus who wrote about 400 books during his long life. Only about thirty-six of these books still exist today. He mostly wrote about Islamic law and the history of different religions.

Ibn Tufayl was an Andalusian philosopher and doctor. He wrote Hayy ibn Yaqzan, a unique book that combines story and philosophy. This work later inspired Daniel Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe.

In 1248, the Christian King, Ferdinand III of Castile, took control of Seville. The Spanish historian Américo Castro wrote that when the victorious Christian soldiers first saw Seville, they were completely amazed. In fact, the city’s public works, economy, and culture offered a level of development that the Christian world had never seen before.

exercises.title: Notice: Who Did It?
exercises.instructions: Sort the sentences: is the doer named, or not named?
exercises.question: When does the book name the doer?

items: Madinat al-Zahra Palace was built by Caliph Abd al-Rahman III.
the progress which was made by Muslims
commentaries written by Muslim scholars and philosophers
The lands under Muslim rule were known as Al-Andalus.
Many people were sent into exile.
Arabic was the official language and schools taught in it.

The doer is named (by …): Madinat al-Zahra Palace was built by Caliph Abd al-Rahman III.
the progress which was made by Muslims
commentaries written by Muslim scholars and philosophers
The doer is not named: The lands under Muslim rule were known as Al-Andalus.
Many people were sent into exile.
Arabic was the official language and schools taught in it.

exercises.explanation: The passive puts the result first. The book adds “by + doer” when the doer is important (Abd al-Rahman III, Muslims, Muslim scholars). When the doer is clear or not important, it leaves it out.

feedback.correct: Good. Some passives name the doer with by; others do not.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the word by.

exercises.title: Notice: Contrast Words
exercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Then choose the best answer.
exercises.question: “Although their lands slowly got smaller after the 11th century, Muslims lived there for 781 years.” Which sentence has the same kind of link?
options: Islamic rule ended in 1492. However, Muslims continued to have an important role in the economy.
Therefore, it was natural that their next move was towards the Iberian Peninsula.
Thanks to his efforts, many Andalusians managed to escape.
exercises.explanation: Although and however both show a contrast: something we do not expect after the first fact. Therefore shows a result, and thanks to shows a positive cause.

feedback.correct: Correct. However also shows a contrast.
feedback.incorrect: Which sentence has a surprise after the first fact?

exercises.title: Notice: Not Only … But Also
exercises.instructions: Read the statement. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: In “Not only did different cultures meet, but two different social and economic systems also came together”, the writer adds a second, bigger point.
exercises.explanation: “Not only … but also” adds a second point to the first one. After “Not only” at the start, the verb comes before the subject: “did different cultures meet”.

feedback.correct: Correct. The second point is added to the first.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 3, paragraph 2.

exercises.title: Build: Cause and Result

exercises.question: How does the book link causes and results?
exercises.fillBlanksText: The Visigothic Kingdom faced many problems [blank] internal struggles for the throne. [blank] these problems, Muslims conquered the country very easily. Church leaders thought the process was too slow. [blank], they established the Inquisition.
exercises.explanation: “Due to” and “because of” come before a noun. “As a result” starts a new sentence and gives the result of the sentence before.

feedback.correct: Well done. Due to, Because of, As a result.
feedback.incorrect: Before a noun: due to / because of. At the start of a result sentence: As a result.

feedback.correct: Correct. To choose, to find, realize.
feedback.incorrect: Which verb takes to, and which takes the base verb after a person?

feedback.correct: Correct. Andalusia, one of Spain’s 17 autonomous regions.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 1.

the Umayyad governor of Ifriqiya

feedback.incorrect: Find Córdoba in Chapter 3.

exercises.title: Uniting the People
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the book supports.
exercises.question: What did Abd al-Rahman III do to reduce the power of the old Arab nobles?
options: He gave important positions to Christian slaves and Berbers instead of Arabs.
He sent the nobles to North Africa.
He made peace with the Fatimids.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “Abd al-Rahman III used foreign fighters in his army and gave important positions in the government to Christian slaves and Berbers instead of Arabs. By doing this, he successfully reduced the power of the traditional Arab nobles.”

feedback.correct: Correct. He gave positions to other groups.
feedback.incorrect: Find “By doing this” in Chapter 5.

sequencingItems.text: Abd al-Rahman III claimed the title of caliph.
